messages:
From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
To: Evan Li <evan@stathub.ai>, Samantha Rogers <samantha.rogers@stathub.ai>
Cc: Alex Martinez <alex_martinez@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, Grace O'Connor <grace_oconnor@redwood.ai>
Date: Sun, 17 May 2026 09:03:00 -0700
Subject: Stathub renewal — proposed staged provisioning to blunt May/June spikes

Evan / Samantha,

Thanks again for the detailed usage exports. We've run the last 90 days through our capacity model and there are two things I want to put on your radar before the renewal:

- The observed 95th percentile token throughput in late-April/early-May is ~1.6x the contract baseline for the highest-consuming routes.
- Short (2–6 hour) daily spikes correlate with your data-prep pipelines hitting concurrency windows; those are the primary driver for peak GPU load.

Recommendation (high level): staged provisioning — reserve an initial +15 GPUs for the renewal term, with an automated 14-day surge attenuation policy that allows for temporary burst to an additional 10 GPUs before falling back. This reduces tail latency risk while keeping committed capacity steady.

I've attached the capacity_model_v3.xlsx and the usage_snapshot_may2026.csv showing the spike distribution. Proposed SOW language is in SOW_draft_v2.pdf — it includes a short pilot period and a 30-day observability window for tuning batching/caching settings.

Next steps I'd suggest:
1) We (Redwood) align on the exact GPU types and placement (hosted vs dedicated pool) — Ben and Alex can propose node mixes.
2) Stathub confirms whether burst costs are acceptable or should be capped — if capped, we'll propose a prioritized route list to protect latency-sensitive traffic.
3) Sign pilot addendum; we can spin capacity within 7 business days after PO.

Can we schedule a 30-min call tomorrow to walk through the numbers? I'm free 10–12 PT.

Thanks,
Ben

Subject: RE: Stathub renewal — staged provisioning suggestion

Ben — good analysis. A couple of operational notes before we land on numbers:

- For renewals we prefer committing on a GPU-hour baseline rather than an absolute GPU count when there's heavy burst behavior; that gives Stathub predictable unit economics while we absorb transient spikes.
- If we go the +15 reserved route, recommend the initial pool be 90% A100-80GB equivalent (for encoder-decoder workloads) + 10% L4/ovx for cheaper embedding-heavy routes.

I've updated the SOW placeholder to include a 60-day observability clause (helps engineering lock batching thresholds) — see comment in SOW_draft_v2.pdf. Also added an SLA exception clause for scheduled model refreshes.

Alex — can you draft the node mix and a short fallback policy (prioritized route list and burst cap defaults)? I can then iterate terms with procurement.

Marissa

Ben / Marissa / Alex,

Appreciate the analysis and the suggested guardrails. A few quick questions from our side:

1) Can you show estimated incremental monthly cost for the +15 reserved + 10 burst scenario vs a straight +20 reserved? We want to compare predictable commit vs burst headroom.
2) On the burst attenuation policy — what happens to in-flight requests if we hit the burst cap? Is there graceful degradation or model fallback?
3) For the pilot period, can we scope a single high-risk route (the 2nd-stage comparator) rather than the whole account? That will shorten the tuning window.

We are comfortable with the 60-day observability clause, but procurement will ask for the incremental cost delta before we sign. Can you also provide a short note about how you recommend we set TTLs for prefix caching so the burst impact is minimized?

Thanks — happy to hop on a call Thursday if useful.

VP Engineering, Stathub AI

Subject: RE: Stathub renewal — staged provisioning suggestion

Evan / Samantha — thanks for the thoughtful questions. Answers below and next steps at the bottom.

1) Cost comparison: see the attached capacity_model_v3.xlsx, tab 'cost_comparison'. Quick summary (rounded):
   - +15 reserved + 10 burst (burst pay-as-you-go): ~$32,400/mo incremental
   - +20 reserved (flat commit): ~$44,800/mo incremental
   Savings come from moving the most frequent but non-peak hours into the burst tier and keeping the commit smaller. We'll send a per-route breakdown separately.

2) Burst attenuation behavior: when the burst cap is reached the system executes the prioritized route list. Higher-priority (latency-sensitive) routes get fallback to a smaller-model variant we host (compatible quantized variant) while lower-priority routes are queued up to a short backpressure window (max 8s) before we return a 503. We can also configure automatic retries and a gradual shedding policy to avoid an immediate cliff. We'll document exact behavior in the SOW appendix.

3) Pilot scope: agree that scoping to your 2nd-stage comparator route is the right short test. We'll provision the staged pool for that route only and run a 30-day tuning window; if we meet the latency SLOs we'll roll the configuration account-wide.

Action items / timeline:
- I will attach a small per-route cost spreadsheet and a one-page TTL recommendation for prefix caching (aim for 5–20s for ephemeral prefixes; extend to 2–5m for stable user prefixes).
- Marissa to iterate SOW terms with procurement (add the per-route cost appendix).
- Ben to book a technical kickoff for next Wed (May 26) to run the pilot runbook.
- Stathub to confirm PO preference (burst-enabled vs flat commit) by Tue May 25.

I'll drop the per-route cost CSV into the Drive link and ping you both. If you want a call Thurs at 10 PT, Ben and I can join, otherwise we'll go asynchronous.

Thanks,
Alex Martinez
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
